newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau eyes 1999 handover to China "with acceptance".
newsitem.headline: Macau eyes 1999 handover to China "with acceptance".

text.p: While political disputes rock Hong Kong over the British colony's return to China, the Portuguese enclave of Macau is looking to its own handover three years from Friday with quiet acceptance, analysts and residents said.
"Look at the map and you know Macau is part of China," jewellery trader Leung Sio Fong said on Friday, echoing the feelings of many Macau residents, most of whom are ethnic Chinese.
Like its neighbour Hong Kong, tiny Macau is preparing to become a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China.

On December 20, 1999, General Vasco Rocha Vieira will step down as the last Lisbon-appointed governor after nearly 450 years of Portuguese administration and Macau's 424,000 residents will start a new era under Beijing's wing.
"The Macau handover is much smoother and less politically controversial than the Hong Kong case," political analyst Sonny Lo of the University of Hong Kong told Reuters.
"Macau has already become a de facto Chinese territory even though it is still administered or ruled by the Portuguese. Chinese influence in Macau is very great -- much greater than in Hong Kong."
Unlike the British in Hong Kong, the Portuguese have sought China's assent on all major policy decisions and infrastructure projects. Lisbon has been praised by Chinese officials for its cooperation.
On Thursday, Vieira said his administration would "do everything within its reach" to prepare the enclave for 1999.

Beijing has said Macau's 23-member legislature -- made up of eight directly elected members, eight indirectly elected members and seven appointees -- will ride through the handover and sit until the legislators' five-year terms expire in 2001.
Candidates representing three election groups from the powerful gambling, property and entertainment sectors won four of the elected seats in September's poll.
The 14-day campaign was dogged by rumours of bribery and vote-buying.
Analysts and some community leaders have voiced concern that the rumoured irregularities indicated organised crime syndicates were seeking influence in Macau's political system.

The Macau SAR will have at the helm a Chinese chief executive chosen by Beijing-appointed committees to replace the outgoing Portuguese governor. Analysts expect the selection process to take place in late 1998 or early 1999.
While most observers see popular banker-cum-legislator Edmundo Ho Hua Wah at the top of the list, others say a dark horse could emerge.
Ho has said he is not interested in running for the top job.

Macau's selection bodies and chief executive would have similarities to their counterparts in nearby Hong Kong as they were likely to be drawn from the enclave's business community, the University of Hong Kong's Lo said.
"The selection committee in Macau will likely be dominated by businesspeople, just like the case in Hong Kong," he said.
"Macau's people tend to accept the reality that there will be businesspeople ruling Macau, and basically the pro-democracy voice there is very, very weak."

A Selection Committee of prominent Hong Kong residents, drawn mostly from the business community, last week chose shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa as the British territory's post-colonial chief executive.
The Beijing-appointed, 400-member committee meets in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Saturday to pick an interim legislature that will replace Hong Kong's elected legislators after the handover.
